facts.text: FAA seat-certification guidance provides a non-accident example of simulation giving false confidence.
facts.quote: The FAA guidance provides a smaller, non-accident example.

facts.text: One validation comparison in FAA guidance had a peak error of only 0.3% but a time-history error of 60.4%.
facts.quote: One validation comparison has only 0.3% peak error but 60.4% time-history error

facts.text: For the FAA validation comparison with 0.3% peak error and 60.4% time-history error, validating only the peak would have led a team to judge the model excellent while missing a major temporal disagreement.
facts.quote: a team validating only the peak would have judged the model excellent while missing a major temporal disagreement.

facts.text: A head-injury model discussed in FAA guidance satisfied the specified validation comparisons but showed a non-conservative tendency.
facts.quote: a head-injury model satisfied the specified validation comparisons but showed a non-conservative tendency

facts.text: Because a validated head-injury model showed a non-conservative tendency, the FAA limited its future use to cases with an expected HIC below 840, rather than permitting use up to the regulatory HIC limit of 1,000.
facts.quote: the FAA limited its future use to cases with an expected HIC below 840 rather than allowing use up to the regulatory HIC limit of 1,000.

facts.text: Passing a validation check did not give the FAA head-injury model unlimited predictive authority.
facts.quote: Passing a validation check did not create unlimited predictive authority.
